newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels show no interest in Cuban asylum offer.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels show no interest in Cuban asylum offer.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori flew home from the Caribbean early on Tuesday with an asylum offer from Cuba for Peru's Marxist hostage-takers, but without any sign the rebels might agree to end the crisis that way.
Cuban leader Fidel Castro's offer to take the roughly 20 rebels holding the Japanese ambassador's home was one of the biggest boosts Fujimori has received so far in the crisis.

The proposal drew immediate backing from Tokyo, whose cooperation is essential to any solution for the 72 VIP captives enduring a 77th day under the gun of Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.
Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters on Tuesday that he had instructed Terusuke Terada, the top Japanese diplomat in Lima, to meet Fujimori as soon as possible.
"After hearing (Terada's) report, we must work towards creating an international atmosphere and international opinion (favorable to the plan)," Hashimoto said in Tokyo.
He did not elaborate, but government sources said his remarks indicated that he would seek support from the United States, an avowed enemy of Cuba, for the proposal.
Top Japanese government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama insisted that the plan would be an effective way to resolve the crisis.
"I will not say whether this is morally right or wrong," Kajiyama told a news conference. "I think it is an effective way both in terms of not giving in to terrorism and of ending this peacefully."
But the key issue remained whether the rebels would agree.

The MRTA's international spokesman, Isaac Velazco, quickly poured cold water on the idea, implying that the diplomatic moves were pointless and premature. "We are not thinking about leaving Peru," he told reporters in Pamplona, Spain, shortly after the asylum offer was announced.

An eighth round of talks between the government and 20-odd MRTA rebels also contrasted strongly with the optimism over the asylum plan and showed the all-party agreement needed prior to such a deal stayed elusive.

Guarantors overseeing the talks said after the meeting late Monday between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and MRTA second-in-command Rolly Rojas that both sides were just digging in behind their bargaining positions.

"The commission of guarantors can indicate that both sides are completing their proposals, which without encompassing agreement will clearly establish their positions," said a downbeat communique read by Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, one of three guarantors.
There was no word on Tuesday from the rebels inside the residence, where police began the day with their customary blaring of music from loudspeakers aimed at the compound.

In Havana on a surprise visit on Monday, Fujimori announced that Castro had agreed to grant asylum if all sides agreed to a way out of Latin America's longest-ever hostage siege. "Cuba is willing to cooperate in the framework for this asylum but not to participate as a mediator," Fujimori said.

The two presidents cut an incongruous pair. Castro is the region's only communist ruler, while Fujimori is an avowed free-market proponent who has spent a large part of his six years in office hunting down communist guerrilla groups.
Castro confirmed that he would accept the MRTA fighters out of "moral duty" and "not a question of convenience."
Fujimori arrived in Lima on the presidential jet in the early hours of Tuesday morning. But he left the military airport without comment to waiting reporters.
The president was due to meet Palermo later on Tuesday for a debriefing on talks with the MRTA, which are slated to continue on Wednesday at a safe house near the besieged residence.

The MRTA's main demand is for the release of some 400 of their comrades from Peruvian prisons. Fujimori has flatly ruled this out, although he has offered an asylum deal and hinted at other concessions that analysts say may include improved prison conditions and trial processes.
